cues.text:
In 1889, the 300-metre Eiffel Tower became
one of the main attractions
at the World's Fair in Paris.

How did an exhibition landmark become part
of military communications?

Nine years later, engineer Eugène Ducretet
sent a Morse code signal

from the tower to the Panthéon, a building
about four kilometres away.

Short and long signals travelled through
the air.

No telegraph wire was needed between the
two buildings.

But that experiment linked two points
within one city.

The French Army needed radio communication
between Paris and the fortresses
on the country's eastern border.

Long-distance communication required
powerful transmitters,
sensitive receivers and tall antennas.

The Eiffel Tower's height could prove
useful.

In 1903, Paris officials discussed
redeveloping the Champ de Mars,
where the tower stood.

They considered removing it, but the city
decided to keep the structure.

Separate from that decision, Gustave
Eiffel made the tower available

to military engineer Gustave Ferrié for
radio research
and helped fund the work.

Ferrié and his team placed the equipment
in a wooden room
near the south pillar.

They attached antennas high on the iron
structure.

The first long-distance messages reached
forts in eastern France.

The headquarters could contact the
fortifications by radio,

without a telegraph line between the
points.

Later, a radio link was established with
Bizerte —
a naval base in what is now Tunisia.

A signal from France crossed the
Mediterranean.

In 1909, a permanent military radio
station was installed
on the Champ de Mars.
Its equipment was placed underground.

Above the station rose the tower,
whose height now helped military radio

communication — though it had first been
built for an entirely different purpose.
